tagline: From the Norman Conquest to Chaucer — a three-stage diploma in reading the language of the Canterbury Tales and Sir Gawain.
philosophy: Middle English sits between Old English and modern English, closer to us in grammar but foreign in spelling and sound. The great vowel shift has not yet happened; the final -e is still pronounced; French and Latin have flooded the vocabulary. We teach it as a language to be read with notes and heard aloud. You will earn the right to sit down with Chaucer, the Gawain poet, Langland, and Julian of Norwich — to read them in the manuscripts' spelling (or near enough) with a glossary and a grammar at your side. That is the goal.
duration_estimate: 4–8 months at one hour per day
method: Reading-led, with heavy emphasis on pronunciation and meter. Chaucer's verse only makes sense when you hear it aloud. Grammar is simpler than Old English (no four-case system, much less inflection) but spelling is wild. Every lesson contains lines from the Canterbury Tales or Gawain.
prerequisites: None. A passing familiarity with Chaucer in modern English translation helps but is not required.

stages.name: The Sound and the Shape
stages.subtitle: Pronouncing the final -e, the great vowel shift not yet complete, Chaucer's meter; reading aloud before parsing.
learning_outcomes: Read aloud any printed Middle English text with accurate reconstructed pronunciation (London dialect, c. 1380–1400).
Pronounce the final -e when required by meter or grammar and recognize when it is silent.
Distinguish the Middle English vowel values from modern English (fyre sounds like modern 'feere,' not 'fire'; name sounds like 'nahm-uh,' not 'name').
Hear and reproduce the French-influenced consonants (ch, j, sh, th, v, z) and the surviving Old English yogh (ȝ).

lessons.title: The Alphabet and Spelling Chaos
lessons.content: Twenty-six letters as in modern English, plus the yogh (ȝ) in some manuscripts. Spelling varies by scribe. The same word appears as 'though,' 'thogh,' 'þogh,' 'þow.' You learn to recognize patterns, not rules.

lessons.title: The Vowels Before the Shift
lessons.content: Long a = 'ah' (name = NAH-muh). Long e = 'ay' (sweet = SWAYT). Long i = 'ee' (fyre = FEE-ruh). Long o = 'oh' (good = GOHD). Long u = 'oo' (hous = HOOS). Short vowels closer to modern.

lessons.title: The Final -e
lessons.content: Pronounced as a separate syllable (schwa) when: 1) required by meter, 2) after a single consonant following a short vowel, 3) in the dative singular of nouns, 4) in the plural of weak verbs. Silent otherwise.

lessons.title: Consonants and the Yogh
lessons.content: Ch = 'ch' as in church. J = 'j' as in judge (new from French). Th = 'th' voiced or unvoiced. V and F distinguished (Old English had only F). Yogh (ȝ) = 'y' or guttural 'gh.' The letter thorn (þ) disappears; scribes use 'th' instead.

lessons.title: Stress and Meter
lessons.content: Chaucer writes iambic pentameter. Five beats per line, alternating unstressed and stressed. The final -e counts as a syllable when you need ten syllables; drops when you have ten without it.

lessons.title: First Lines
lessons.content: Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote... — the opening of the Canterbury Tales. Read it aloud ten times, attending to every final -e. WHAHN thaht ah-PREEL with hiss SHOO-res SOH-tuh...

lessons.title: Ten Common Words
lessons.content: hir (her, their), hem (them), swich (such), yif (if), eek (also), biforn (before), wyf (wife, woman), knyght (knight), soothly (truly), ful (very, full). Practice pronunciation and spelling recognition.

checkpoint.title: Stage 1 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Twenty words read aloud and recorded; ten lines of Chaucer scanned for meter and final -e; five modern English words transliterated into Middle English spelling patterns. Pass mark: 85%.

stages.name: The Sentence
stages.subtitle: Much simpler grammar than Old English — closer to modern but with archaic forms; the verb, the noun, the pronoun.
learning_outcomes: Recognize and parse the major Middle English verb forms (infinitive, present, past, past participle, subjunctive).
Decline the personal pronouns in all cases (I/me/my; thou/thee/thy; he/him/his; she/hir/hir; we/us/our; ye/you/your; they/hem/hir).
Translate sentences of the form Subject + Verb + Object with prepositional phrases, relative clauses, and a genitive of possession.
Read one-hundred-word passages from Chaucer and the Gawain poet with notes.

lessons.title: The Infinitive and the Present Tense
lessons.content: Infinitive ends in -en (loven, riden, singen) or -e (love). Present: I love, thou lovest, he loveth, we loven, ye loven, they loven. The third-person singular -eth (or -th) is the mark of Middle English.

lessons.title: The Past Tense — Weak Verbs
lessons.content: Loved, loved, loved. The -ed suffix as in modern English. Pronounced as separate syllable when meter requires.

lessons.title: The Past Tense — Strong Verbs
lessons.content: Riden becomes rood (singular) or riden (plural). Singen becomes sang or sungen. The old ablaut patterns survive from Old English but simplified.

lessons.title: The Past Participle
lessons.content: Strong verbs: y- prefix optional (riden or y-riden), vowel change from infinitive (sungen, comen, goon → gon). Weak verbs: loved.

lessons.title: The Subjunctive
lessons.content: Present subjunctive often identical to infinitive (that he love, that they come). Past subjunctive: were, hadde, mighte. Used in conditions, wishes, commands, subordinate clauses after 'that.'

lessons.title: The Verb 'To Be'
lessons.content: I am, thou art, he is, we been/are, ye been, they been. Past: I was, thou were, he was, we were. Irregular, essential.

lessons.title: Pronouns — Personal
lessons.content: Thou (singular, intimate or inferior) versus ye (plural or formal singular). The great shift from thou to you happens after Chaucer. Hir (their) and hem (them) come from Old Norse; Old English would have used hira and him.

lessons.title: Pronouns — Relative and Demonstrative
lessons.content: That, which, who (but 'who' still rare as a relative pronoun in Chaucer; 'that' is more common). This, that, thise, tho (those).

lessons.title: Nouns and the Genitive
lessons.content: Plural: add -es or -s. Genitive (possessive): add -es or -s. The four-case system of Old English is gone. The knightes tale = the knight's tale. The knightes = the knights.

lessons.title: Adjectives
lessons.content: No inflection except occasional weak forms after 'the' (the yonge sonne, the olde man). Comparatives: -er, -est. Irregular: good/bettre/beste, yvel/worse/worste.

lessons.title: Negation
lessons.content: Ne + verb, often reinforced with nat or noght. He ne dorste nat (he dared not). Double and triple negatives are emphatic, not incorrect.

lessons.title: Word Order and Style
lessons.content: More flexible than modern English. Verb-subject inversion common after adverbs (Thanne longen folk to goon...). French influence: adjective sometimes follows noun (chivalrye royal).

lessons.title: Reading: The General Prologue, Lines 1–18
lessons.content: Whan that Aprill... to Thanne longen folk to goon on pilgrimages. The opening verse paragraph. Full grammatical commentary on every line.

lessons.title: Reading: The Knight's Tale, Lines 859–882
lessons.content: The description of the temple of Mars. Chaucer's high style. Latinate vocabulary and complex syntax.

checkpoint.title: Stage 2 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Written. Conjugate five verbs in present and past; parse twenty inflected forms; translate a one-hundred-word passage from Chaucer with notes. Pass mark: 80%.

stages.name: The Reading
stages.subtitle: The General Prologue, lines 1–100, and selections from Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. The capstone.
learning_outcomes: Read and translate the first one hundred lines of the General Prologue to the Canterbury Tales in the original.
Read and translate selections from the first fitt of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (the Green Knight's entrance and challenge, lines 136–231).
Recognize and explain the difference between Chaucer's London dialect and the Gawain poet's Northwest Midlands dialect.
Discuss in writing the literary and metrical character of the two texts.
Translate any passage of forty or fewer words from a glossed Middle English text at sight.

lessons.title: The General Prologue, Lines 1–42
lessons.content: The opening: the spring, the pilgrims, the narrator's voice. Line-by-line close reading. Vocabulary: shoures soote, croppes, foweles, corages, palmeres, strondes, seke, halwes, couth.

lessons.title: The General Prologue, Lines 43–78
lessons.content: The description of the pilgrims begins. The Knight, the Squire. High style, courtly vocabulary. Vocabulary: worthy, chivalrye, trouthe, honour, bataille, viage, Alisaundre, lustier, bacheler.

lessons.title: The General Prologue, Lines 79–100
lessons.content: The Yeoman, the Prioress introduced. Transition from martial to ecclesiastical estates. Vocabulary: pecok arwes, bracer, gay daggere, yemanly, cloistre, charitable, pitous, Eglentyne, coral, gauded.

lessons.title: Chaucer's Vocabulary — French and Latin Layers
lessons.content: Germanic core (go, come, good, man, wife). French overlay (courtesy, honour, service, gentle, royal). Latin learned words (devout, compassion, conscience, piteous). You learn to hear the register.

lessons.title: Chaucer's Meter and Rhyme
lessons.content: Iambic pentameter, rhyming couplets (heroic couplets). Enjambment rare; each couplet tends to close a thought. Caesura mid-line. Practice scansion on ten couplets.

lessons.title: Sir Gawain — Dialect and Spelling
lessons.content: Northwest Midlands dialect, c. 1380–1400. Spelling differs from Chaucer: quen (when), quyl (while), schulde (should), -3 (yogh) for -gh or -y. Pronunciation differs slightly.

lessons.title: Sir Gawain — Alliterative Meter
lessons.content: Not iambic pentameter. Long alliterative lines as in Old English, grouped in stanzas ending with a rhymed 'bob and wheel' (short line + four-line rhymed tail). The meter of Beowulf brought forward six hundred years.

lessons.title: Sir Gawain, Lines 136–159
lessons.content: The Green Knight's entrance into Arthur's hall. Ther hales in at the halle dor an aghlich mayster... — 'There hastens in at the hall door a terrible master.' Vocabulary: aghlich, mayster, enker, grene, semblaunt.

lessons.title: Sir Gawain, Lines 160–183
lessons.content: The description of the knight and his horse. Al grene, with grene stele and grene enamayl... Reading the color symbolism and the French/English lexical mix.

lessons.title: Sir Gawain, Lines 184–207
lessons.content: The Green Knight speaks. His challenge: I craue in this court a Crystemas gomen... — 'I crave in this court a Christmas game.' Close reading of the courtly speech register.

lessons.title: Sir Gawain, Lines 208–231
lessons.content: Arthur's response; Gawain volunteers. Bot Arthur wolde not ete til al were serued... Close reading of the social dynamics and the chivalric code.

lessons.title: Alliterative Vocabulary
lessons.content: Gawain's poet loves rare and archaic words (burne = man, lede = man, hathel = hero, renk = man, tulk = man). Five synonyms for 'man' in fifty lines. The lexical richness of the alliterative tradition.

lessons.title: Comparison: Chaucer and Gawain
lessons.content: Chaucer: London, French-influenced, iambic, rhymed, written for reading aloud at court. Gawain: Northwest Midlands, more conservative, alliterative, written for a regional aristocratic audience. Both c. 1380–1400. The two great streams of late medieval English verse.

lessons.title: Sight Reading Practice
lessons.content: Five short passages (thirty to forty words each) from Langland's Piers Plowman, Julian of Norwich's Revelations, and the York mystery plays, with glosses but no grammatical notes. The student parses and translates at sight.

checkpoint.title: Stage 3 Capstone Examination
checkpoint.format: Written, three hours. Translate the General Prologue lines 1–100 with notes. Translate Sir Gawain lines 136–231 with notes. Translate one forty-word sight passage from a glossed Middle English text. Write a short essay (three hundred words) comparing the meter and diction of Chaucer and the Gawain poet. Pass mark: 70%. Honors: 85%.

certification.credential_name: The Kalopaideia Diploma in Reading Middle English
certification.credential_subtitle: An attestation that the bearer has completed the three-stage course and passed the capstone examination.
certification.what_it_is: A privately-issued certificate of completion. Not an academic degree. Not a teaching license. It says: this person sat down with Chaucer and the Gawain poet and earned an honest reading of them.
certification.what_is_recorded: Student's chosen public name; the language; the date of the capstone examination; the result (Pass or Pass with Honors); the SHA-256 hash of the student's signed examination scripts.
certification.what_is_not_recorded: The actual examination answers; the student's email or other identifiers; anything that could identify the student against their will. The certificate is pseudonymous if the student wishes.
certification.issuance: On-chain on Base as an ERC-721 soulbound (non-transferable) token. One certificate per student per language. The contract is owned by Kalopaideia and the minting key is held by the proprietor. The token URI points to a permanent, IPFS-pinned JSON document signed by Kalopaideia's issuing key.
certification.verification: Any third party can verify a certificate at kalopaideia.com/verify/<token-id> by entering the token ID and the certificate hash. The page will display the issuance date, the language, and the result.
certification.cost: Included in the Akousma subscription. The on-chain gas fee at issuance is paid by Kalopaideia. The student pays nothing extra.
certification.renewability: None. A diploma is not a driver's license. Once earned, it stands.
